lesson.title: The High Frontier: The Cold War in Orbit
lesson.summary: When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, it triggered an American crisis of confidence and a Cold War competition for space that culminated in the United States landing astronauts on the Moon in 1969.
lesson.body:
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth, a beach ball sized sphere that did little more than transmit a steady radio beep. The technical achievement mattered less than what it implied: the same rocket powerful enough to launch a satellite into orbit was powerful enough to deliver a nuclear warhead across continents, connecting this new competition directly to the arms race already underway between the two superpowers. Sputnik triggered something close to panic in the United States, where many Americans had assumed their country led the world in science and technology, and the shock, sometimes called the Sputnik crisis, led Congress to pass the National Defense Education Act in 1958 to fund science and math education and push more resources into research.

The United States moved quickly to catch up. It launched its own first satellite, Explorer 1, on January 31, 1958, and that same year Congress created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA, signed into law by President Eisenhower on July 29, 1958, to coordinate American efforts in space. The Soviets kept scoring firsts, though, launching the dog Laika into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 in November 1957 and then sending the first human into space, cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, on April 12, 1961, a feat the United States matched only weeks later when astronaut Alan Shepard made a brief suborbital flight on May 5, 1961.

Stung by the Soviet lead, President John F. Kennedy addressed Congress on May 25, 1961, and committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade, a bold and enormously expensive goal at a time when American spaceflight experience amounted to a few minutes above the atmosphere. The resulting Apollo program consumed vast resources and scientific effort throughout the 1960s, driven not by any pressing military or scientific necessity but by the conviction that leading in space demonstrated the superiority of the American system over Soviet communism to the entire watching world.

The United States met Kennedy's deadline on July 20, 1969, when Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first human being to walk on the Moon, describing the moment as "one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." The Space Race stands as one of the more constructive expressions of Cold War rivalry: rather than fighting directly, as they had by proxy in Korea, the two superpowers channeled their competition into scientific and engineering achievement, producing genuine advances in technology even as the underlying rivalry that funded them remained rooted in the same distrust that had defined the Cold War since its origins in the 1940s.
